source.title: The Heterogeneous Safety Impacts of Benign Multilingual Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Will Hawkins; Kai Rawal; Jonathan Rystrøm; Stratis Tsirtsis; Zi-Hao Fu; Greta Warren; Ryan Brown; Eoin Delaney; S. Wachter; Brent D. Mittelstadt; Christopher Russell

record.tranche_reason: Tests benign fine-tuning of instruction-tuned models and measures compliance with adversarial harmful prompts, using a multilingual extension of the fine-tuning and safety-evaluation approach.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SORRY-Bench compliance outcomes after benign fine-tuning, including figure-only results, numerical hyperparameter-ablation results, and a mechanistic analysis. Results from cited studies are not included. Values used only to select the 80th-percentile layer and other analysis settings are not recorded as outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained instruct models with LoRA on 1,000 benign Dolly-seeded examples, as in the original benign-tuning setup. It then measures SORRY-Bench harmful compliance against the base models. The multilingual extension adds a new setting, but the English FT / English eval conditions match the original question directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also stress that English-only fine-tuning and evaluation give inadequate safety assurance, and that small models are especially vulnerable. They add that small representational drift from non-English tuning pushes models toward exaggerated compliance or refusal, depending on architecture.
record.recipe_differences: Benign instruction tuning with LoRA and adversarial-compliance evaluation are close to the original approach, but this study uses 1,000 examples, multilingual training and evaluation, and small instruction-tuned model families rather than testing only the original setting.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, fine-tuning language, evaluation language, number of epochs, and LoRA scaling ratio. The study reports changes between α/r = 2 and α/r = 8 and between English and local-language evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: Relation between safety-direction displacement (80th-percentile layer) and change in English adversarial compliance is architecture-dependent. Small drift goes with more compliance in Llama and more refusal in Gemma-3-4B/Qwen3-4B, with no consistent relation in the tiny Gemma and Qwen models. English FT produced the largest drift but stayed closest to baseline compliance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: After benign fine-tuning, the link between hidden-state safety-direction drift and harmful compliance depends on architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Primary results in Figure 1 are shown as figures and averaged across three seeds; the text does not provide most individual rates or uncertainty estimates. The experiments focus mainly on small models and one-epoch tuning, and the authors note translation-quality concerns for Irish and some output-language mismatches. The Qwen3-0.6B reductions may reflect capability degradation.
record.rows_left_out: Additional one-epoch language/model rates in Figures 1-2, three- and five-epoch outcomes in Appendix Figures 5-6, larger-model outcomes in Appendix Figure 10, and capability and translation-quality metrics were not individually extracted. The selected text provides no per-condition numeric values for most of these figure-only results; the reported prose summaries and the Table 2 ablations are retained.

untested.parts: Full-parameter fine-tuning; models above 4B are only in an appendix figure; data chosen to be maximally damaging (e.g., identity-shifting or selected benign subsets) was not tested; only one dataset size (1,000).
No per-token KL or position-wise analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Hidden-state direction drift is measured, but there is no weight/rank localization test.
No test of why alignment is shallow.

missing.what: Gemma-3-4B-IT local-language evaluations generally show sharp compliance increases after non-English FT (only the Portuguese case is recorded).
Exceptions: Gemma-3-1B-IT Irish FT did not show the increase; Qwen3-0.6B Chinese FT did not show the decrease.

Larger models (α/r=2): Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct English-eval compliance rose, more after English than Hindi FT; Qwen-8B/14B compliance fell. The prose gives directions even though values are figure-only.
Authors state that a small amount of FT undoes most alignment for Gemma-3-1B and Llama-3.2, and that 5 epochs drove compliance to zero (collapse).

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T1 is chosen because the English-FT conditions mirror Qi et al.'s benign-tuning setup; the multilingual conditions are a T3-style extension. Table 2 α/r=8 values coincide with the main configuration, so H rows partly duplicate Figure 1 conditions. Qwen3-0.6B reversals are confounded by apparent model collapse, so the challenge from that model is weaker than the raw numbers suggest. Base rates differ greatly between models (Qwen3-0.6B starts at 83.2% EN compliance).

versions.untested_parts: The paper uses benign fine-tuning data, not harmful fine-tuning examples.

Tests benign multilingual fine-tuning with 1,000 examples and LoRA; does not test the claimed range of a few to a few hundred examples or establish that harmful compliance is raised for all models and conditions.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
Measures hidden-state safety-direction drift, but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test why safety would be shallow or whether a data or training objective produces shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to spread safety beyond the first response tokens.
